explanations.answer: Why no one talks of restoring the king
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The people say Absalom, the man they anointed, has died in battle. Then comes the question: “So why do you say nothing about restoring the king?” It's a group chat where everybody keeps typing and nobody hits send.

explanations.answer: Who they should anoint as king next
explanations.explanation: Nobody here is shopping for a new king. Absalom, David's son, is the one they anointed, and he has died in battle. What the people ask is why nobody is saying anything about restoring the king, and that king is David.

explanations.answer: Whether to go fight the Philistines
explanations.explanation: The Philistines only come up as part of what David did for them. The people say he delivered them from the hand of the Philistines. No new battle is on the table. The people are asking why nobody is talking about restoring the king.

Judah is right. David sends this message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, and it's for the elders of Judah. He asks why they should be the last to restore the king to his palace. I think the sting is in the word "last." Nobody wants to be last in line.

Ephraim isn't named in this message. David tells the priests to speak to the elders of Judah. He asks why they should be the last to restore the king to his palace. So the question lands on Judah's doorstep.

Dan doesn't show up in this message at all. David has Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, carry his words to the elders of Judah. That's who gets asked why they'd be the last to restore the king. Dan is off the guest list this time.

explanations.answer: They are his own flesh and blood
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. David says, “You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood.” Then he asks again why they should be the last to restore the king. He sounds like a man at a family reunion saying, "Come on, it's ME!"

explanations.answer: They swore to serve him forever
explanations.explanation: David mentions no sworn promise here. What he says is, “You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood.” He's reaching for family, not for a vow. I think it's a warm way to knock on a door.

explanations.answer: Their land belongs to the king
explanations.explanation: Land never comes up in this message. David talks about family: “You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood.” Then he asks why they should be the last to restore the king. He's asking as a brother, not a landlord.

Commander is the word. David says, “…if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab!” Amasa, who led Absalom's army (2 Samuel 17:25), is being offered the top spot. That's a promotion with a mustache-sized wow attached.

David isn't handing Amasa a money job. He says Amasa will be commander of his army in place of Joab. Joab is the one who has been leading David's army (2 Samuel 8:16). Nobody here is counting coins, they're leading troops.
No pen and parchment for Amasa. David swears he'll be the commander of his army in place of Joab. Amasa is the man who led Absalom's army (2 Samuel 17:25). It's a sword job, not a desk job.
Close, but it went the other way. The text says David “swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man.” No half and half here. They all sent word to the king together.
You called it, baker. The text says David “swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man.” That's the opposite of split. They all sent word to the king with one voice.
That's the message. The men of Judah send word to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.” Two words and the whole mood flips. After all that arguing, that's the sweetest text David could get.
Judah isn't telling David to wait. They send word right away: “Return, you and all your servants.” No waiting on a vote from anybody. It's an invitation, and it's open now.

Amasa isn't part of Judah's reply. David had a message for him, but what Judah sends back is: “Return, you and all your servants.” They want the king himself, not a go-between. I think that's a pretty clear welcome.

explanations.answer: To escort the king across the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's it. The men of Judah came to Gilgal “to meet him and escort him across the Jordan.” They aren't waiting at home, they come out to the river. That's like showing up at the airport instead of texting "safe travels."

explanations.answer: To stop the king from crossing over
explanations.explanation: Nobody's blocking the road. The men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and escort him across the Jordan. They had just sent word saying, “Return.” You don't send that and then slam the gate.

explanations.answer: To hand Amasa over to the king
explanations.explanation: No handoff of Amasa here. The men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and escort him across the Jordan. Amasa's promotion was a message David sent, not a delivery. The Jordan crossing is all about getting David home.
Yes, baker. Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite from Bahurim, came down along with a thousand men of Benjamin. He didn't come alone. That's a crowd arriving behind him.
It's true, actually. Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down along with a thousand men of Benjamin. He brought a whole crowd. So don't picture one lonely man at the river.

explanations.answer: Ziba the steward of Saul's house
explanations.explanation: That's him. Ziba, the steward of the house of Saul, rushed down to the Jordan with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. That's thirty-six people if you count Ziba, which is a lot of people to carry up to a river. He wasn't coming by himself.

explanations.answer: Hushai the friend of the king
explanations.explanation: Hushai isn't named at the Jordan here. Hushai, the Archite, is called David's friend (2 Samuel 15:37). In this scene, the one with fifteen sons and twenty servants is Ziba, the steward of the house of Saul. Hushai isn't in the headcount.

Ittai doesn't appear in this crossing. He's the Gittite who led a third of David's troops (2 Samuel 18:2). The man rushing down here with fifteen sons and twenty servants is Ziba, the steward of the house of Saul.

explanations.answer: He falls down before the king
explanations.explanation: That's what he does. When Shimei crossed the Jordan, he fell down before the king. No hiding, no hanging back. The man goes straight to the ground.

explanations.answer: He stands back and keeps quiet
explanations.explanation: Shimei isn't standing back. He crosses the Jordan, falls down before the king, and speaks. His words come right after. There's no quiet corner in this scene.

Hiding isn't the plan. A thousand men of Benjamin came with him, but Shimei crosses the Jordan and falls down before the king. Then he says, “…here I am today.” That's a man stepping forward, not ducking behind a crowd.

Right. Shimei says, “My lord, do not hold me guilty, and do not remember your servant's wrongdoing on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem.” He asks the king not to take it to heart. It's a hard thing to ask, and he asks it from the ground.

explanations.answer: To give him a place at court
explanations.explanation: No job request here. Shimei asks the king not to hold him guilty and not to remember his wrongdoing on the day the king left Jerusalem. He's not asking for a seat at the table.

explanations.answer: To give him back his land
explanations.explanation: Land isn't part of it. Shimei's whole request is about guilt: “…do not hold me guilty…” He also asks the king not to remember his wrongdoing on the day the king left Jerusalem. That's what he's carrying down to the Jordan.
Not quite. Shimei says the opposite: “For your servant knows that I have sinned…” He talks about his wrongdoing on the day the king left Jerusalem. He doesn't argue his case, he owns it.

Good eye, baker. Shimei says, “For your servant knows that I have sinned…” He names his wrongdoing on the day David left Jerusalem. No excuses, no spin. That's about the hardest sentence to say out loud.

It goes the other direction. Abishai son of Zeruiah, one of David's commanders (2 Samuel 18:2), asks, “Shouldn't Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?” That's not a plea for mercy. He's asking for the opposite.

That's right. Abishai son of Zeruiah, one of David's commanders (2 Samuel 18:2), asks, “Shouldn't Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?” He wants Shimei put to death. Mercy is David's answer, not Abishai's.

explanations.answer: Today he is king over Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes. David asks, “Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” He's saying he knows what day it is. It's the day he comes home as king, and he doesn't want it to be the day somebody dies.

explanations.answer: Today is a holy feast day
explanations.explanation: No feast is mentioned. David says, “Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” That's the thing he knows about today. He doesn't mention a calendar, only his own place as king.
The priests aren't part of this answer. They carried David's message earlier, but here David says, “Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” He's speaking for himself, as king.
That's the word. The king says to Shimei, “You shall not die.” Shimei had come down on his face, and these are the words he gets. I think that's a sentence he'll remember for a long time.
The king doesn't say "return." He says to Shimei, “You shall not die.” Abishai had asked whether Shimei should be put to death, and this is David's answer. It settles the question.
David isn't telling Shimei to be quiet. Shimei has already spoken, and the king answers, “You shall not die.” The question was whether he'd be put to death. The king says no.
You've got it. After telling Shimei, “You shall not die,” the king swore an oath to him. A king's word, with an oath on top. That's the promise nailed down twice.
Actually, he did. The text says the king swore an oath to Shimei after telling him, “You shall not die.” So it wasn't just a passing sentence. David put an oath behind it.
